title: 1 Samuel 23:1–14
context: While Saul hunts him, David rescues the Judean town of Keilah from Philistine raiders after inquiring of the LORD twice. Abiathar, the priest who escaped Saul’s massacre at Nob (22:20), arrives with the ephod. When Saul plans to trap David inside the walled town, David asks the LORD whether Saul will come and whether Keilah will hand him over, and he leaves when told they would. Saul searches daily, but God does not give David into his hand.

verses.text: David was told, “Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah, and are robbing the threshing floors.”
verses.arminianNotes: Keilah is under attack, and David hears of it while he is himself a fugitive. Arminian readers note that David’s first instinct is to care for others in danger, a willing response to need that shows the shepherd heart God values in a leader.
verses.reformedNotes: The Philistines rob the threshing floors at harvest time, threatening the town’s food supply. Reformed readers see David acting as the true protector of God’s people while the reigning king pursues him, a contrast that points to the kingship God has chosen.

verses.text: Therefore David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I go and strike these Philistines?” The LORD said to David, “Go strike the Philistines, and save Keilah.”
verses.arminianNotes: David inquires of the LORD before acting, and the LORD tells him to go and save Keilah. Arminian readers see a model of prayer that seeks God’s guidance in a real decision, where David is free to obey and the outcome depends on that obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that God directs David’s steps and promises deliverance before the battle. The word save Keilah casts David as God’s instrument of rescue, anticipating his role as the anointed king.

verses.text: David’s men said to him, “Behold, we are afraid here in Judah. How much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?”
verses.arminianNotes: David’s men are afraid, already hunted in Judah and now asked to face the Philistines too. Arminian readers take their fear seriously and note that God answers honest doubts with further assurance rather than rebuke.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that fear arises when people measure the task by their own strength. The men’s question sets the stage for God to show that the outcome rests on his promise, not their numbers.

verses.text: Then David inquired of the LORD yet again. The LORD answered him, and said, “Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks again, and the LORD answers with a stronger promise: I will deliver the Philistines into your hand. Arminian readers see God’s patience with his servants’ need for reassurance, meeting them where they are.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God condescending to his people’s weakness, confirming his word a second time. The repeated inquiry shows that seeking God’s will is not a lack of faith but its exercise.

verses.text: David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines, and brought away their livestock, and killed them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
verses.arminianNotes: David and his men defeat the Philistines and save Keilah’s inhabitants. Arminian readers note that obedience leads to real deliverance for others, as the faithful response of David’s band becomes the means of rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: The verse repeats that David saved Keilah, echoing God’s command in 23:2. Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled exactly, with David’s victory attributed to the LORD’s promise.

verses.text: When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech fled to David to Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, comes with an ephod after escaping the slaughter at Nob (22:20-23). Arminian readers note that God preserves a faithful priest who now becomes a channel of guidance for David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see providence in the timing: the priest who survived Saul’s violence brings the means of inquiry to the one God has chosen. Saul, who killed the priests, has cut himself off from such guidance.

verses.text: Saul was told that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, “God has delivered him into my hand, for he is shut in by entering into a town that has gates and bars.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says God has delivered David into his hand because he is shut in a walled town. Arminian readers see a man reading events to fit his own desires, claiming God’s support for what God has not approved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony: Saul uses the language of providence, but 23:14 says plainly that God did not deliver David into his hand. Interpreting providence apart from God’s word leads to self-deception.

verses.text: Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah to besiege David and his men.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul summons all the people to besiege Keilah, the town David had just saved. Arminian readers see the tragedy of a king turning the nation’s strength against the man who protected it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul is willing to endanger an Israelite town to capture one man. His obsession shows how a heart set against God’s purpose turns even royal power toward destruction.

verses.text: David knew that Saul was devising mischief against him. He said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
verses.arminianNotes: David learns of Saul’s plan and asks Abiathar to bring the ephod. Arminian readers note that David does not rely on his own judgment but seeks God’s direction through the appointed means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David using the means God provided, the priest and the ephod, rather than guessing or acting in panic. Wise action rests on seeking God’s word.

verses.text: Then David said, “O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah to destroy the city for my sake.
verses.arminianNotes: David’s prayer lays out the threat honestly: Saul seeks to destroy the city because of him. Arminian readers note his concern for the people of Keilah as well as himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David addresses God as the LORD, the God of Israel, and calls himself your servant. His prayer combines reverence, humility, and a clear statement of need.

verses.text: Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? LORD, the God of Israel, I beg you, tell your servant.” The LORD said, “He will come down.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks two questions: will Keilah hand him over, and will Saul come? God answers the second first: he will come down. Arminian readers see God giving real information that allows David to make a free and wise decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God answers truly about what Saul intends, yet the event never happens because David leaves. The answer concerns what would occur if David stayed, a point that leads to the discussion at the next verse.

verses.text: Then David said, “Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul?” The LORD said, “They will deliver you up.”
verses.arminianNotes: David repeats the question about Keilah, and God says they will deliver him up. Arminian readers see God’s knowledge of what free people would do in a situation, offered as a gracious warning so that David can avoid it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that God truly knew what the men of Keilah would do and warned David graciously. They see the answer as an instance of God’s perfect knowledge serving his purpose to preserve his anointed.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions agree that God truly knew what Saul and the men of Keilah would do if David stayed, that his answer was a real and gracious warning, and that the outcome did not occur because David acted on it. Some Arminian thinkers, along with Molinists, cite this text as an instance of middle knowledge: God’s knowledge of what free creatures would do in any circumstance, logically prior to his decree. Arminius himself is often noted in scholarship as using this category, though many Arminians do not adopt Molinism. Reformed theologians generally affirm that God knows such conditionals but typically reject middle knowledge as independent of his decree, grounding it in his natural knowledge of all possibilities and in his will. Some readers in both traditions hold that the passage shows God’s knowledge of the conditional without settling the philosophical question.

verses.text: Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed out of Keilah and went wherever they could go. Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah; and he gave up going there.
verses.arminianNotes: David and about six hundred men leave Keilah and go wherever they can. Arminian readers note that David acts on the warning, so God’s word leads to a real change in what happens.
verses.reformedNotes: Saul gives up going to Keilah once he hears David has escaped. Reformed readers see God’s warning working exactly as intended: the conditional outcome is averted, and David is kept safe.

verses.text: David stayed in the wilderness in the strongholds, and remained in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul sought him every day, but God didn’t deliver him into his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: David stays in the wilderness strongholds while Saul seeks him daily. Arminian readers note the hardship of a life on the run, and David’s continued trust despite it.
verses.reformedNotes: God didn’t deliver him into his hand answers Saul’s boast in 23:7. Reformed readers see this as the key interpretive line: behind the daily chase stands God’s sovereign protection of David.
